13.1. And Belisarius about the summer solstice went against Wittigis and the camp of the Goths, leaving some few in Rome for the sake of a garrison, but bringing all the rest with himself. 13.2. And sending some men to Tudera and Clusium, he ordered them to make stockades, since he intended to follow them and to help besiege the barbarians there. 13.3. And they, when they learned that the army was advancing, did not withstand the danger but sent envoys to Belisarius and promised to surrender both themselves and each city by agreement, on condition that they should remain unharmed. And when he arrived they fulfilled their promise. 13.4. And he, removing all the Goths from there, sent them to Sicily and Naples, and establishing a garrison in Clusium and Tudera, led the army forward. 13.5. In the meantime Wittigis, sending another army and Vacimus as commander to Auximus, ordered them to mingle with the Goths there, and with them, going against the enemy in Ancon, to make trial of the fort there. 13.6. Now this Ancon is a certain elbow-shaped rock, from which it has received this name; for it is for the most part like an elbow (ankon). 13.7. And it is distant about eighty stades from the city of Auximus, of which it is the port. And the fortification of the fort lies in safety on the elbow-shaped rock, but all the buildings outside, though they are many, 13.8. were from of old without a wall. And Conon, who had been set over the guard of the place, as soon as he heard that Vacimus and his men were advancing and were already not far off, made a display of unreasoning judgement. 13.9. For thinking it a trifling matter to preserve the fort and its inhabitants together with the soldiers unharmed, he left the fortification altogether destitute of soldiers, and leading them all out about five stades, he drew them up as if for a pitched battle, not making the phalanx deep, but so as to surround the whole foot of the hill as if for a hunt. 13.10. And these, when they saw the enemy far surpassing them in numbers, turning their backs, fled straightway to the fort. 13.11. And the barbarians, pursuing, killed there most of them, all who did not succeed in getting inside the wall, and setting ladders against the wall, made trial of the ascent. And some set fire to the houses outside the fort. 13.12. And the Romans who also before had dwelt in the fort, struck with consternation at the present situation, opening the postern before, received the soldiers as they fled in no order. 13.13. And when they saw the barbarians pressing close upon the fugitives, fearing lest they should burst in along with them, they quickly shut the gates, and letting down nooses from the battlements, they drew up and saved some others and Conon himself. 13.14. The barbarians, however, going up by the ladders, came near to taking the fort by force, had not two men, displaying marvellous deeds, thrust back by their valour those who had already got onto the battlements—of whom the one was a guard of Belisarius from Thrace, Ulimuth by name, and the other of Valerianus, Gouboulgoudou, 13.15. a Massagete by race. For these two men had by some chance sailed in a little before to Ancon; and in this struggle, defending themselves with their swords against those who came up, they saved the fort contrary to expectation, but were themselves carried off from there half-dead and with their whole bodies hacked. 13.16. At that time it was reported to Belisarius that Narses had come from Byzantium with a large army and was in Picenum. Now this Narses was a eunuch and steward of the royal treasures, but otherwise keen and more energetic than would befit a eunuch. 13.17. And five thousand soldiers followed him, of whom others led by companies, and Justinus the general of the Illyrians, and another Narses, a deserter to the Roman manner of life from the Armenians subject to the Persians, who had come previously with his brother Aratius, who had come a little before with another army to Belisarius. 13.18. And there followed him also about two thousand of the nation of the Eruli, whom Visandus and Aluith and Phanitheus commanded.

14.1. Who in the world the Eruli are, and whence they came into alliance with the Romans, I now proceed to tell. They dwelt of old beyond the Ister river, holding the belief in a great throng of gods, whom they thought it holy to propitiate even with sacrifices of human beings. 14.2. And they used many customs not in accordance with those of other men. For it was not permitted them to live when they grew old or fell sick, but whenever one of them was seized either by age or by sickness, it became necessary for him to ask his kinsmen to remove him from among men as quickly as possible. 14.3. And they, heaping up much wood to a great height and seating the man on top of the wood, would send to him one of the Eruli, but a stranger, with a dagger; 14.4. for it was not lawful for the slayer to be a kinsman of his. And when the slayer of their kinsman returned, they straightway burned all the wood, beginning from the edges. 14.5. And when the flame had ceased for them, gathering the bones, they immediately hid them in the earth. 14.6. And when an Erulian man died, it was necessary for his wife, if she laid claim to virtue and wished to leave a good name for herself, to die not long afterward by fastening a noose beside the tomb of her husband. 14.7. And if she did not do this, it remained for her for the future to be without repute and to have given offence to the kinsmen of her husband. Such, then, were the customs the Eruli used of old. 14.8. But as time went on, having become superior in power and in numbers to all the barbarians around them, and attacking, as was natural, 14.9. they conquered each in turn and by force plundered them. And at last they made the Lombards, who were Christians, and certain other nations subject to themselves in the payment of tribute—a thing not customary to the barbarians there, but they had been led to it by love of money and by arrogance. 14.10. When, however, Anastasius took over the empire of the Romans, the Eruli, having no men left against whom they could go, laid down their arms and remained quiet, and a period of three years was spent by them in this peace. 14.11. And they, being exceedingly distressed, reviled their ruler Rodulphus without restraint, and going constantly to him, called him soft and womanish, and abused him in no orderly fashion with certain other names, taunting him. 14.12. And Rodulphus, bearing the insult by no means well, marched against the Lombards who were doing no wrong, neither bringing any charge of fault against them nor pretending any breaking of the agreements, 14.13. but bringing a war that had no cause. And when the Lombards learned of this by report, sending to Rodulphus, they inquired and saw fit to ask the reason for which the Eruli were going in arms against them, agreeing that, if they had withheld anything of the tribute, they would pay it at once with much added; but if they complained that the tribute set for them was moderate, the Lombards would never be slow to make it greater. 14.14. These things the envoys offered, but Rodulphus dismissed them with a threat and drove forward. And they again, sending other envoys to him, entreated and besought much concerning the same things. 14.15. When these second envoys too had been sent away, a third embassy coming to him forbade the Eruli to bring upon them a war without pretext. 14.16. For if those men should go against them with such a purpose, they too, not willingly but as being most compelled, would array themselves against the attackers, calling God to witness, of whose inclination even the very slightest weight at all would be set against all the power of men; and it was likely that he, being moved by the causes of the war, would adjudge for both the issue of the battle. 14.17. These things they said, thinking thereby to frighten the attackers, but the Eruli, holding back nothing of all, resolved to come to close quarters with the Lombards. 14.18. And when both armies had come close to each other, it came about that the air above the Lombards was covered by a black and exceedingly thick cloud, while above the Eruli there was prodigious clear sky. 14.19. From which, judging by signs, one would have guessed that the Eruli were going to the engagement to their own harm; for there can be no more bitter portent for barbarians setting themselves to battle than this. 14.20. The Eruli, however, did not even pay attention to this, but altogether disregarding it, with much contempt advanced against the enemy, measuring the issue of the war by the multitude of their throng. 14.21. But when the battle was at close quarters, many of the Eruli were killed, and Rodulphus himself was killed, and all the rest fled with all their might, mindful of no resistance. 14.22. And as the enemy pressed close upon them, most of them fell there, but some few were saved. 14.23. Wherefore they could no longer remain in their ancestral abodes, but removing from there as quickly as possible, they kept going forward, traversing the whole land which is beyond the Ister river, together with their children and wives. 14.24. And when they came to a region where the Rogi anciently dwelt, who, having mingled with the army of the Goths, had gone into Italy, there they settled. 14.25. But when they were oppressed by famine, since the land was deserted, removing from there not long afterward, they came close to the country of the Gepaedes. 14.26. And the Gepaedes at first, when they had become suppliants, permitted them to settle and be neighbours to them. 14.27. Then they began, from no cause, to display unholy deeds toward them. For they did violence to their women and seized their oxen and other goods, and they left out no act of injustice at all, and finally began to lay unjust hands upon them. 14.28. And the Eruli, no longer able to bear these things, crossed the Ister river and resolved to dwell near the Romans there, Anastasius holding the imperial power, who received them with much friendliness and permitted them to settle there. 14.29. But not long afterward these barbarians gave offence to him, having wrought unholy deeds against the Romans there; wherefore he sent an army against them. 14.30. And the Romans, conquering them in battle, killed most of them, and had it in their power to destroy them all. 14.31. But the survivors of them, having become suppliants of the generals, begged both to be preserved and to be henceforth allies and servants of the emperor. 14.32. And when Anastasius learned this it pleased him, and from this it came about that some of the Eruli were left, though they neither became allies of the Romans nor did them any good. 14.33. But when Justinian took over the empire, presenting them with good land and other goods, he was able to make them altogether his friends and persuaded them all to become Christians. 14.34. Wherefore, changing their mode of life to the more gentle, they resolved to go over for the most part to the laws of the Christians, and in alliance for the most part they array themselves with the Romans against the enemy. 14.35. They are, however, still faithless toward them and, being gripped by greed, are eager to do violence to their neighbours, 14.36. the deed bringing them no shame. And they perform unholy unions, both with men and with asses, and they are the basest of all men and, being evil, are destined to perish evilly. 14.37. Afterward a few of them remained in treaty with the Romans, as shall be written by me in the subsequent narrative; but all the rest revolted from the following cause. 14.38. The Eruli, displaying the beastlike and frenzied quality of their character against their king (this man was Ochus by name), suddenly killed the man from no cause, bringing no other charge than that they wished for the future to be without a king. 14.39. And yet even before this the king had the name among them, but carried off almost nothing more than any private man whatever. 14.40. But all saw fit both to sit together with him and to be his messmates, and without restraint anyone who wished insulted him; 14.41. for there are no men more faithless or more unstable than the Eruli. And when the evil had been wrought by them, they now repented. 14.42. For they said they were not able to live without a ruler or without a general; so after much deliberation it seemed altogether better to them to summon one of the royal line from the island of Thule. And what this is I shall presently make plain.

15.1. When the Eruli, defeated in battle by the Lombards, removed from their ancestral abodes, some of them, as has been related by me before, settled in the regions in Illyricum, but the others resolved by no means to cross the Ister river, but settled in the very extremities of the inhabited world; 15.2. these, then, with many of the royal blood leading them, traversed in succession all the nations of the Sclaveni, and crossing a wide deserted country from there, came to the people called the Varni. 15.3. After them they passed by the nations of the Danes, the barbarians there not doing them violence. 15.4. And coming thence to the ocean, they took ship, and putting in at the island of Thule, remained there. Now Thule is exceedingly large; for it happens to be more than ten times greater than Britain. 15.5. And it lies far from it toward the north wind. In this island the land is for the most part deserted, but in the inhabited part thirteen most populous nations are settled, and there are kings over each nation. 15.6. There a marvellous thing happens every year. For about the summer solstice the sun for about forty days does not set at all, but continuously during all this time appears above the earth. 15.7. But no less than six months later, about the winter solstice, the sun does not appear at all over this island for forty days, but unending night is poured over it; and dejection from this holds the people there during all this time, since they have no means of mingling with one another in the interval. 15.8. For me, then, to go to this island and to be an eye-witness of the things told, though I was eager, in no way came about. 15.9. From those who came to us from there, however, I inquired in what way they were able to reckon the measure of the days, when the sun neither rises nor sets at the appropriate times there. And they told me an account both true and trustworthy. 15.10. For they say that the sun during those forty days does not set, as has been said, but appears to the people there now toward the east, now toward the west. 15.11. So whenever, coming round again and being near the horizon, it reaches the same place where they had before seen it rising, they reckon that thus one day and one night have passed. 15.12. And whenever the time of the nights comes, judging always by the courses of the moon and the stars, they reckon the measure of the days. 15.13. And when a period of thirty-five days has run by in this long night, certain men set out to the summits of the mountains—for this is customary with them—and seeing the sun somehow from there, they announce to the people below that within five days the sun will shine upon them. 15.14. And the whole people hold a festival of good tidings, and this in darkness. And this is the greatest of the festivals for the Thulitae; 15.15. for these islanders, it seems to me, are always exceedingly afraid, although the same thing happens to them every year, lest the sun should at some time fail them altogether. 15.16. But of the barbarians settled in Thule one nation only, who are called the Scrithiphini, have a beastlike mode of life. For they neither put on garments nor walk with shoes, nor do they drink wine nor have any eatable thing from the earth. 15.17. For they neither till the earth nor do their women work anything for them, but the men, always together with the women, practise hunting alone. 15.18. For a great quantity of wild beasts and other animals the forests bear for them, being prodigiously great, and the mountains that rise there. 15.19. And they always feed on the flesh of the beasts caught and clothe themselves in their skins, since they have neither flax nor any tool with which they might sew; but binding the skins of the beasts to one another with their sinews, they thus cover their whole body. 15.20. Nor indeed do they rear their infants in the same way as other men. 15.21. For the children of the Scrithiphini are not fed with the milk of women, nor do they touch their mother's breast, but they are reared on the marrow alone of the animals caught. 15.22. So whenever a woman has given birth, putting the infant into a skin, she straightway hangs it upon some tree, and placing marrow in its mouth, she sets out with her husband to the accustomed hunt. For in common with him they do all things and pursue this occupation. 15.23. Such, then, is the manner of life of these barbarians. The other Thulitae, however, almost all, so to speak, differ in nothing greatly from other men; but they worship many gods and demons, of the heaven and the air, of the earth and the sea, and certain other divinities said to be in the waters of springs and rivers. 15.24. And they sacrifice continually all kinds of victims and make offerings to the dead, but the finest of their victims is a human being, whom they make captive in war first; 15.25. for him they sacrifice to Ares, since they consider him the greatest god. And they sacrifice the captive not only by slaying him, but also by hanging him from a tree and casting him into thorns, and killing him by other most pitiable forms of death. 15.26. Thus the Thulitae live. Of them one populous nation is the Gauti, beside whom at that time the immigrant Eruli settled. 15.27. And now the Eruli who dwell among the Romans, the murder of their king having been wrought by them, sent some of their notable men to the island of Thule, to search out and bring back, if they should be able to find anyone there of the royal blood. 15.28. And when these men had come to the island, they found many there of the royal line, but selecting one who pleased them most, they set out on the return journey with him. 15.29. But he, when he had come among the Danes, died of sickness. Wherefore these men, coming again to the island, brought back another, Datius by name. And his brother Aordus followed him, and two hundred youths of the Eruli in Thule. 15.30. And as much time was being spent by them in this journey, a thought came to the Eruli about Singidunum that they were not doing what was advantageous to themselves in bringing a leader from Thule, against the will of the emperor Justinian. 15.31. So sending to Byzantium, they begged the emperor to send them a ruler, whoever should be his choice. 15.32. And he straightway sent to them one of the Eruli who from of old had his residence there, Suartuas by name. 15.33. Him the Eruli at first saw and did obeisance to gladly, and obeyed as he gave the customary orders; but not many days later one came announcing that those from the island of Thule were somewhere close. 15.34. And Suartuas ordered them to go to meet them, in order to destroy them, and the Eruli, approving the plan, straightway followed. 15.35. But when they were a day's journey apart from each other, all of them by night deserting him went over to the newcomers, while he himself fled alone to Byzantium. 15.36. And the emperor with all his might set himself to restoring him to power, but the Eruli, fearing the power of the Romans, resolved to go over to the Gepaedes. This, then, was the cause of the revolt of the Eruli.

16.1. And Belisarius and Narses with both their armies joined each other about the city of Firmum, which lies along the shore of the Ionian Gulf and is distant a day's journey from the city of Auximus. 16.2. There with all the commanders of the army they deliberated whither it would be more advantageous for them to go first against the enemy. 16.3. For if they should go against those besieging Ariminum, they suspected that those in Auximus, coming behind them, would, as is likely, do irreparable harm both to themselves and to the Romans dwelling there; and they feared for the besieged, lest they should suffer something terrible from the want of necessities. 16.4. Now the most of them, being angry at John, made their speeches. For they reproached him because, by unreasoning rashness and by love of much money, he had come to such danger, and did not allow the operations of the war to be carried on in order or as Belisarius directed. 16.5. But Narses (for John was the dearest of all men to him), fearing lest Belisarius, yielding to what had been said by the commanders, should put the affairs at Ariminum in second place, spoke as follows: 16.6. “You are deliberating, men in command, not about the usual matters, nor do you hold counsel about things concerning which one might reasonably be in doubt, but about matters in which it is possible even for those who have come to no experience of war to choose offhand the better course. 16.7. For if the danger seemed to be equal and the harm to those who failed equal on either side, it would be worth while to deliberate sufficiently and, going to the greatest length of calculation, thus to make the decision concerning the present situation. 16.8. But we, if we should wish to put off the assault on Auximus to some other time, shall in no way suffer loss in essential matters; for what difference would there be in the interval? But at Ariminum, if, as is likely, we fail—not to put it too bitterly—we shall undo the strength of the Romans. 16.9. So if John has insulted your instructions, most excellent Belisarius, you have taken a great penalty from him, since it is in your power both to save the man who has erred and to give him over to the enemy. 16.10. But beware lest you take from the emperor and from us the penalties for the things in which John, through ignorance, has erred. For if the Goths now take Ariminum, it will come about that an energetic Roman general and a whole army and a city subject to the emperor have been made captive. 16.11. And the danger will not stop at this, but they will be able to overturn the whole fortune of the war. For reckon thus concerning the enemy, that in multitude of soldiers they still even now far surpass us, but they have fallen into a cowardice from the disasters in which they have often failed. And with reason; for the opposition of fortune has taken from them all their boldness. 16.12. If, then, they prosper at the present time, they will not long afterward recover their spirit, and for the rest will carry on this war not only with daring equal to ours, but with much greater. 16.13. For those who escape from difficulties are wont always to have better hopes than those who have not yet met with misfortune.” Narses said so much. 16.14. And a certain soldier, escaping the guard of the barbarians from Ariminum, came to the camp and showed Belisarius a letter which John had written to him. 16.15. And the writing made plain the following: “Know that all the provisions have long since failed us, and that for the future we are not able either to hold out against the populace or to defend ourselves against the assailants, but within seven days we shall, unwillingly, hand over both ourselves and this city to the enemy; 16.16. for to force the present necessity further we are by no means able—a necessity which to make our defence on our behalf, if we should do anything not seemly, 16.17. I think sufficient.” Thus John wrote. And Belisarius was at a loss and fell into great perplexity. For he both feared for the besieged and suspected that the enemy in Auximus would ravage all the regions there more boldly, going about them, and would lie in ambush for his camp from behind, especially whenever they should come to grips with their opponents, and would, as is likely, work much irreparable harm. 16.18. After this, however, he did as follows. He left Aratius there with a thousand men, on condition that they should make a camp by the sea, two hundred stades distant from the city of Auximus. 16.19. And he ordered them neither to remove from there and go elsewhere nor to fight with the enemy, except in so far as they defended themselves from their camp, if those men should ever go against them. 16.20. For in this way he hoped that the barbarians especially, since the Romans were encamped somewhere close to Auximus, would remain quiet and would never follow to do them mischief. 16.21. And he sent a most considerable army with ships, of which Herodian and Uliaris and Narses the brother of Aratius were in command. 16.22. And supreme over the fleet was Ildiger, whom Belisarius instructed to sail straight for Ariminum, taking care not to attempt to put in at the shore there while the foot-army was left far behind; for they were to journey not far from the coast. 16.23. And he ordered another army, of which Martinus was in command, to go along by the seacoast keeping pace with these ships, instructing them, whenever they should come near the enemy, to burn many fires, not in proportion to the army, and to give their opponents the impression of a multitude much greater. 16.24. And he himself, with Narses and the rest of the army, went by another road furthest from the coast, through the city of Urbisalia, which in former times Alaric so destroyed that nothing whatever of its former adornment is left to it, except a single gate and a small remnant of the foundations of its ground-plan.

17.1. Here it befell me to see a sight of the following kind. When the army with John came into Picenum, there was, as was natural, much confusion among the people there. 17.2. And of the women, some fled suddenly wherever it had become possible for each, while others, being caught, were carried off in no orderly fashion by those who fell in with them. 17.3. In one of these places a certain woman who had just given birth happened to have left her child lying on the ground in its swaddling-clothes, and whether fleeing or caught by someone, she was no longer able to return there; for it befell her plainly to have vanished either from among men or from Italy. 17.4. So the child, left in this solitude, kept weeping. And a single she-goat, seeing it, took pity on it and, coming near (for she too happened to have just given birth), gave it the teat and guarded the child carefully, 17.5. lest a dog or some wild beast should harm it. And as much time was spent in the confusion, it came about that the child shared in this teat for a long while. 17.6. And when it became known to the people of Picenum afterward that the emperor's army had come there for the harm of the Goths, but that the Romans would suffer nothing unpleasant from it, 17.7. they all returned home straightway. And when in Urbisalia the women had come with the men, all who were Roman by race, when they saw the child surviving in its swaddling-clothes, being unable to account for what had happened, they were in great wonder that it lived. 17.8. And each one offered her teat who happened to be in a suitable condition for this. But the child would no longer take human milk, and the goat was by no means willing to let it go, but bleating most continually about the child, she seemed to the bystanders to be doing dreadful things because the women, coming close to the child, were thus troubling it, and to put it in a word, she laid claim to the infant as her own. 17.9. And from this the women no longer troubled the child, and the goat reared it more fearlessly and, taking care of it otherwise, guarded it. Wherefore the people of the place called this child Aegisthus. 17.10. And when it befell me to be present there, making a display of the marvel, they used to bring me to the child and on purpose, 17.11. in order that it might cry, troubled it. And it, distressed by those who troubled it, wept, and the goat, hearing it (for she was distant from it about a stone's throw), at a run and bleating loudly came to it, and coming and standing over it, took her stand, so that no one might be able to trouble it for the rest of the time. Such, then, are the things about this Aegisthus. 17.12. And Belisarius advanced through the mountains there. For being far surpassed in numbers by his opponents, he was not willing to come to close quarters with them in the open, since he saw too that the barbarians were resolved to die in their encounters; 17.13. and he thought that they, as soon as they should learn that an army of the enemy was advancing against them from all sides, would be mindful of no resistance, but would straightway turn to flight. And he hit upon the true opinion, having suspected nothing far from what was to be. 17.14. For when they had come into the mountains, about a day's journey distant from Ariminum, they fell in with a few Goths who were travelling by the road on some errand. 17.15. And these, falling unexpectedly upon an army of the enemy, were by no means able to turn aside from the road, until, being shot at by those who went in front, some of them fell there, while others, having become wounded, ran up onto some of the cliffs there and escaped notice. 17.16. From there, observing the Roman army pouring into all the difficult places, they supposed them to be far more than the true measure. 17.17. And there, seeing also the standards of Belisarius, they knew that he was leading this army. And night came on, and the Romans bivouacked there, while the wounded among the Goths went secretly to the camp of Wittigis. 17.18. And coming there about midday, they showed their wounds and affirmed that Belisarius with an army greater than could be numbered would presently be at hand. 17.19. And they were preparing as if for battle, turned toward the north wind of the city of Ariminum (for there they supposed the enemy would arrive), and they all kept looking continually toward the heights of the mountain. 17.20. But when, night having come on for them, they laid down their arms and were resting, they saw many fires to the east of the city, about sixty stades off, which the army with Martinus was burning, and they came into helpless fear; 17.21. for they suspected they would be encircled by the enemy at daybreak. So this night they bivouacked in such fear, and on the following day, with the sun rising, they saw a fleet of ships coming against them, prodigious in size; and falling into speechlessness, they rushed into flight. 17.22. And packing up quickly, they were held by so great a tumult and shouting that they neither heard the orders given nor took anything else into their mind than how each one might first get away from the camp and get inside the wall of Ravenna. 17.23. And if there had happened to be any strength or courage left to the besieged, they would have sallied out and killed very many of the enemy there, and the whole war would have ended there. 17.24. But as it was, this was prevented both by the great fear that had come upon them before and by the weakness, befalling many through the want of necessities. So the barbarians, by the excess of their tumult leaving some of their goods there, ran at full speed toward Ravenna.

18.1. And first of the Romans, Ildiger and his men, coming to the camp of the enemy, made into the account of slaves those of the Goths who, held by some sickness, had remained there, and gathered all the goods which the Goths had left in their flight. 18.2. And Belisarius came with the whole army at midday. And when he saw John and his men pale and terribly squalid, hinting at the unreasoning quality of his rashness, he said that John owed thanks to Ildiger. 18.3. But he said he owed acknowledgement not to Ildiger but to Narses the steward of the emperor, hinting, I suppose, that Belisarius was not very willing, but had been persuaded by Narses to help them. And for the future the two used much suspicion toward each other. 18.4. Wherefore the friends of Narses would not even allow him to campaign with Belisarius, but persuaded him how shameful it would be for one who shared the secrets of the emperor not to be supreme commander of the army, but to obey a general. 18.5. For they declared that Belisarius would never willingly command the army on equal terms with him, but that, if he wished to lead the Roman army by himself, more soldiers and far better ones, with their commanders, would follow. 18.6. For they said that the Eruli and the guards and shield-bearers of Belisarius himself, and those whom Justinus and John himself commanded, together with the followers of Aratius and Narses, were no fewer than ten thousand, men brave and exceedingly good in matters of war, and that they wished that the conquest of Italy should be reckoned not to Belisarius alone, but that Narses too should bear his share. 18.7. For they thought he had left the company of the emperor not in order that by his own dangers he might strengthen the reputation of Belisarius, but in order that, displaying deeds of intelligence and bravery, he might become renowned among all men, as was likely. 18.8. And yet they said that Belisarius would not even be able to accomplish anything without them for the future. 18.9. For the most of the army which he commanded had already been left in forts and cities which he himself had taken, and they enumerated all in order, beginning from Sicily as far as Picenum. 18.10. And Narses, when he heard these things, was exceedingly pleased at the suggestion, and could neither restrain his thought nor remain in his present position any longer. 18.11. So often, when Belisarius saw fit to undertake some task, he withdrew on various pretexts at various times and rejected the proposal. 18.12. Belisarius, perceiving this, calling together all the commanders, spoke as follows: “I do not seem to myself to think the same things as you, men in command, about this war. 18.13. For I see that you despise the enemy as being altogether defeated. 18.14. But I think that, through this boldness of yours, we shall fall into manifest danger, since I know that the barbarians have been defeated by us not through any cowardice nor through fewness of numbers, but, outgeneralled by forethought and counsel alone, have been turned to flight from here. 18.15. And I fear lest you, being deceived by this untrue opinion, work irreparable harm both to yourselves and to the affairs of the Romans. 18.16. For those who seem to have conquered, lifted up by what has been done, are more easily destroyed than those who have failed contrary to expectation, but for the rest are gripped by fear and much anxiety toward their opponents. 18.17. For carelessness has destroyed some of those who were well established, but toil with care has profited many of the unfortunate. 18.18. Since the power of those who yield to negligence is wont for the most part to be lessened, but practice is naturally sufficient to put strength in. 18.19. Let each of you, then, consider that in Ravenna are Wittigis and many tens of thousands of Goths, and Uraïas is besieging Mediolanum and has surrounded all Liguria, and Auximus is already full of a large army worthy of account, and many other places are guarded against us by barbarians who are a match for us, as far as Urbiventus, which happens to be in the neighbourhood of Rome. 18.20. So that now more than before our affairs stand in danger, since we have fallen into a kind of encirclement by the enemy. 18.21. For I forbear to say that they declare the Franks too are arrayed with them in Liguria, a thing which it is sufficiently worth while for all the Romans to call to mind, not without great fear. 18.22. I say, then, that a part of the army ought to be sent to Liguria and Mediolanum, while the rest for the present should go against Auximus and the enemy there, to accomplish whatever God may grant; and then to manage the other operations of the war in whatever way may seem best and most excellent.” Belisarius said so much. 18.23. And Narses answered as follows: “In other respects, O general, no one would gainsay that all has been spoken by you with truth. 18.24. But to set apart this whole army of the emperor for Mediolanum and Auximus alone I think altogether inexpedient. 18.25. But that you should lead such of the Romans as you wish against these is in no way unfitting; we, however, will win for the emperor the land of Aemilia, which they say the Goths especially lay claim to, and will so throw Ravenna into confusion that you will deal with the enemy near you as you wish, they being shut off from all hope of those who might defend them. 18.26. For if we should choose to besiege Auximus along with you, I fear lest, when the barbarians come out from Ravenna, it may befall us both to be set between two enemies and, being cut off from the necessities, to be destroyed there.” Narses said so much. 18.27. And Belisarius, fearing lest, the Romans going into many parts, the affairs of the emperor should fall to ruin and be confounded by the disorder thence arising, showed a letter of the emperor Justinian which he had written to the commanders of the army. 18.28. And the writing made plain the following: “We have not sent Narses our steward into Italy in order that he should command the army; for we wish Belisarius alone to lead the whole army in whatever way may seem to him best, and it behoves you all to follow him for what is advantageous to our state.” Such, then, was the emperor's letter. 18.29. But Narses, laying hold of the very end of the letter, contended on the contrary that Belisarius was now deliberating for the advantage of the state; wherefore it was not necessary for them to follow him.

19.1. Hearing this, Belisarius sent Peranius with a large army to Urbiventus, in order that they might besiege it, while he himself led the army against Urbinus, a city both strong and having a sufficient garrison of Goths (this is distant a day's journey from the city of Ariminum for an unencumbered man), and there followed him as he led the army both Narses and John and all the rest. 19.2. And coming near the city, they encamped at the foot of the hill in two divisions; for they were not arrayed with one another, but Belisarius and his men held the parts to the east of the city, while Narses and his men held those to the west. 19.3. Now Urbinus lies on a hill, round and exceedingly high. The hill, however, is neither precipitous nor altogether impassable, but only hard to traverse because it is very steep, especially as one goes very close to the city. 19.4. And it has one entrance on the level toward the north wind. So the Romans were arrayed for the siege thus. And Belisarius, thinking that the barbarians would more easily come over to him by agreement, inasmuch as they had been dismayed at the danger, sent envoys to them and, promising that many good things would come to them, exhorted them to become subjects of the emperor. 19.5. So the envoys, coming near the gates (for the enemy did not receive them into the city), said much that was very enticing, but the Goths, bold in the strength of the place and the abundance of provisions, would by no means admit the proposals, but ordered the Romans to depart from there quickly. 19.6. So Belisarius, hearing this, ordered the army to gather thick rods and to make from them a long shed. 19.7. Hiding inside it, they were to go very close to the gates with it, where the ground is most level, and to use it for their plot against the wall. And they did accordingly. 19.8. But some of the friends of Narses, joining him, said that Belisarius was doing endless things and devising the impossible. For John had already made trial of the place, and that too when a few men held the garrison at that time, and had perceived it to be altogether impregnable (and so it was); but he ought to recover for the emperor the regions in Aemilia. 19.9. Persuaded by this suggestion, Narses by night broke off the siege, although Belisarius entreated much both that he should stay there and that they should help take the city of Urbinus together. 19.10. These went quickly to Ariminum with the rest of the army. And Moras and the barbarians, when at daybreak they saw the enemy withdrawn by half, jeered from the wall, taunting those who had remained. 19.11. And Belisarius wished to assault the wall with the army that was left. And while he was deliberating these things, it befell that a marvellous piece of good fortune came about. 19.12. There was a single spring in Urbinus, from which all the inhabitants there drew water. This, drying up little by little of its own accord, was failing. 19.13. And in three days the water so failed it that the barbarians, drawing it up from there with mud, drank it. Wherefore they resolved to come over to the Romans. 19.14. But Belisarius, having by no means learned this, wished to make trial of the wall. And arming the rest of the army he placed them in a circle all about the hill, and ordered some men on the level ground to bring up the shed of rods; 19.15. for so they have been accustomed to call this engine. And they, slipping inside it, kept advancing and dragging the shed along, escaping the notice of the enemy. 19.16. So the barbarians, stretching out their right hands from the battlements, begged to obtain peace. But the Romans, not knowing anything of what had happened about the spring, suspected that they feared the war and the engine. Both sides, then, gladly abstained from the battle. 19.17. And the Goths surrendered both themselves and the city to Belisarius by agreement, on condition that they should remain unharmed, having become subjects of the emperor with the Roman army on equal and like terms. 19.18. And Narses, hearing this, regarded the matter both with wonder and as a misfortune. 19.19. And he himself still remained quiet in Ariminum, but ordered John to lead the whole army against Caesena. And they went carrying ladders. 19.20. And when they came near the fort, they made an assault and tried the wall. But as the barbarians defended themselves stoutly, many others fell there, and Phanitheus the leader of the Eruli. 19.21. And John, having then failed at the fort of Caesena, no longer saw fit to make trial, since it seemed to him impregnable, and with Justinus and the rest of the army drove forward. 19.22. And he took by a sudden assault an ancient city which is named Forocornelius, and the barbarians always withdrawing and by no means coming to close quarters, he recovered the whole of Aemilia for the emperor. These things, then, were carried on thus.

20.1. And Belisarius, when he had taken Urbinus about the winter solstice, thought it inexpedient to go to Auximus immediately; for he suspected that much time would be spent for them in the siege of it. 20.2. For it was impossible to take the place by force because of the strength of its defences, and the barbarians, many and excellent, who held the garrison there, as has been shown by me before, having plundered a large district, had brought in for themselves a great quantity of provisions. 20.3. And he ordered Aratius with a large army to winter in Firmum and to keep watch that for the future the barbarians might not at their will, making sorties from there, more boldly do violence to the regions there; while he himself led the army against Urbiventus. 20.4. For Peranius urged him to this, since he had heard from the deserters that the Goths there were running short of provisions, and he hoped that, if in addition to the want of necessities they should see Belisarius present with the whole army, they would more easily give in; 20.5. which happened. For Belisarius, as soon as he came to Urbiventus, ordered all to encamp in a suitably situated place, while he himself, going about in a circle, looked to see whether somehow it might not be impossible to take it by force. And it seemed to him there was no device for taking the place by force. 20.6. But it seemed to him not altogether impracticable to gain mastery of it secretly through a plot. 20.7. For a certain hill rises alone out of a hollow land, level and flat at the upper parts, but precipitous below. And about the hill rocks of equal height make a kind of encirclement, not being very close, but distant about a stone's throw. 20.8. On this hill the men of old built the city, neither throwing walls around it nor making any other fortification, since the place seemed to them impregnable by nature. 20.9. For there happens to be one entrance to it from the rocks, which, if the inhabitants guard it, they need not fear any assault of the enemy elsewhere. 20.10. For apart from the place where nature has made the entrance to the city, as has been said, a river, always great and impassable, holds the space between the hill and the rocks of which I just made mention. 20.11. Wherefore the ancient Romans made a small building at this entrance. And there is a gate there, which the Goths then guarded. Such, then, is the situation regarding Urbiventus. 20.12. And Belisarius set himself with the whole army to the siege, having the hope either of doing them mischief by means of the river or of reducing the enemy by famine. 20.13. And the barbarians for a while were not altogether in want of the necessities, although they had them in less than sufficient measure; nevertheless they held out against the hardship beyond expectation, by no means coming to fullness of food, but using just so much of victuals each day as not to die of famine. 20.14. But when all the provisions had failed them, they soaked hides and skins in water for a long time and then ate them; for Albilas who commanded them, a man most highly esteemed among the Goths, fed them with empty hopes. 20.15. And when the season, coming round again, brought the summer time, the grain was already at its height in the fields of its own accord, not so much, however, as before, but much less. 20.16. For since it had been hidden in the furrows neither by ploughs nor by the hands of men, but happened to lie on the surface, the earth was able to bring only a small part of it to fruit. 20.17. And as no one reaped it, having come far past its prime it fell again, and nothing thereafter grew from it. And this same thing happened also in Aemilia. 20.18. Wherefore, leaving their homes, the people there went to Picenum, supposing that the regions there, because they were by the sea, would not be altogether oppressed by want. 20.19. And the famine laid hold of the Tuscans too none the less, from the same cause, but all of them who dwelt in the mountains, grinding the acorns of the oaks like grain and making bread from them, ate it. 20.20. And of all kinds of diseases, as was natural, most of them were seized, 20.21. but some, surviving, were saved. In Picenum, however, it is said that no fewer than fifty thousand of the people, Roman farmers, perished of famine, and many more still beyond the Ionian Gulf. 20.22. And of what appearance they became, and in what manner they died, I now proceed to tell, having myself been an eyewitness. 20.23. They became thin and pale, all of them; for the flesh, lacking nourishment, fed, according to the ancient saying, upon itself, and the bile, which now held the mastery over the body by its abundance, gave to these a colour resembling its own. 20.24. And as the evil advanced, all moisture failed them, and the skin, becoming exceedingly dry, was very like leather, giving the appearance of being fixed upon the bones. And changing from livid to black, they resembled torches burnt exceedingly. 20.25. And their faces were always full of amazement, and they always looked terribly somewhat frenzied. And some died from want of food, others even from coming too much to fullness of it. 20.26. For since all the heat which nature kindled within them had been quenched, if anyone fed them to satiety, and not little by little, like infants newly born, these, no longer being able to digest the food, perished much more quickly. 20.27. And some, the famine overpowering them, tasted of one another. And it is said that two women in a certain field above the city of Ariminum ate seventeen men, who happened to be the only ones left in the place. 20.28. For it came about that strangers travelling there lodged in the cottage where these women dwelt; and them, while they slept, the women killed and ate. 20.29. They say, then, that the eighteenth stranger, rising from sleep, just when these women were about to set upon him, leapt up and learned from them the whole story, and killed both of them. 20.30. This, then, they say happened thus. And most, gripped by the necessity of famine, if anywhere any herb chanced to be, would go to it with much eagerness, and kneeling down would try to pull it up from the ground. 20.31. Then (for they were not able, since all strength had failed them) falling over the herb and their hand, they died. 20.32. And no one hid them anywhere in the earth; for there was no one to whom even an account of burial might fall; yet no bird touched them, of which many are wont to feed on dead bodies, 20.33. since they had nothing on which they might rush. For all the flesh, as I have said before, had already happened to be consumed by the famine. Such, then, was the state of things regarding the famine.

21.1. And Belisarius, when he heard that Uraïas and the barbarians were besieging Mediolanum, sent Martinus and Uliaris with a large army against them. 21.2. And they, coming to the river Padus, which is distant a day's journey from Mediolanum, encamped and remained there. And much time was spent by them there, while they deliberated about the crossing of the river. 21.3. And when Mundilas heard this, he sent to them one of the Romans, Paulus by name. 21.4. And he, escaping the notice of the enemy, came to the bank of the Padus. And finding no boat at the moment, he stripped and, swimming, made the crossing at great risk. 21.5. So being brought to the Roman camp and coming to the commanders, he spoke as follows: “Martinus and Uliaris, you are doing things neither just nor worthy of your own reputation, having come in word for the safety of the emperor's affairs, but in deed increasing the power of the Goths. 21.6. For this Mediolanum, which surpasses by far all the cities in Italy in size and in population and in the rest of its prosperity, and apart from these things, being a bulwark against the Germans and the other barbarians and set, so to speak, before the whole Roman empire, has fallen into great danger together with Mundilas and the emperor's army, being troubled by the enemy and neglected by you. 21.7. How greatly the emperor has been wronged by you at the present time, I forbear to say. For the occasion does not allow me to use many words, since I seek some swift help for the city, while there is still some hope left. 21.8. And I say that you ought immediately to defend the Mediolanenses who are in danger. For if you use any delay toward us at the present time, it will come about that we, having suffered the most bitter of all things, shall perish, and that you will have given over the emperor's power to the enemy. 21.9. For traitors, I think, are justly called not only those who throw open the gates to the enemy, but no less, if not more, those who, when it is in their power to defend their dearest who are besieged, choose the safe shrinking instead of the contest and thus give the mastery to the enemy, as is natural.” 21.10. Paulus said so much, and Martinus and Uliaris, promising to follow him immediately, sent the man away. 21.11. And he, again escaping the notice of the barbarians, entered Mediolanum by night, and lifting up the soldiers and all the Romans with hopes, strengthened them still more in their loyalty to the emperor. 21.12. None the less, Martinus and his men, gripped by shrinking, remained there, and much time was spent in this delay. 21.13. And afterward Martinus, wishing to free himself from blame, wrote to Belisarius as follows: “You sent us here to defend those in Mediolanum who are in danger, and we with much eagerness, just as you ordered, have come as far as the river Padus, which the army fears to cross, since we hear that there is a great force of Goths and a very great multitude of Burgundians with them in Liguria, against whom we think ourselves unable to contend alone. 21.14. But order John and Justinus as quickly as possible (for they are in our neighbourhood in the land of Aemilia), together with their followers, to share this danger with us. 21.15. For going from here in common, we shall both be safe ourselves and be able to do some harm to the 21.16. enemy.” So much Martinus's letter made plain. And Belisarius, when he had read it, ordered John and Justinus to go quickly to Mediolanum with Martinus and his men. But they said they would do nothing unless Narses gave them instructions. 21.17. Wherefore Belisarius wrote also to Narses as follows: “Consider the whole army of the emperor to be one body, which, if it does not display one purpose, like the limbs of a man, but wishes to act apart from one another, it will be left to us to perish, having accomplished none of the things that are needful. 21.18. Therefore let Aemilia alone, which has neither any fortification nor brings to the Romans at the present time any weight of advantage. 21.19. But order John and Justinus immediately to go straight against the enemy in Mediolanum together with Martinus and his men, being near and sufficient for the mastery over the barbarians. 21.20. For I have here no multitude of an army which I might send, and besides, I think it inexpedient for soldiers to go to Mediolanum from here. 21.21. For much time will be wasted, so that they will come to it later than the necessary opportunity, and they will by no means be able to use their horses against the enemy, on account of the length of the road, when they come to them. 21.22. But if these men go to Mediolanum together with Martinus and Uliaris, they will both prevail, as is likely, over the barbarians there, and will recover Aemilia again, with no one any longer withstanding them.” 21.23. When Narses saw this letter brought to him, he instructed John and Justinus to go to Mediolanum with the rest of the army. 21.24. And a little later John was sent to the coast in order to bring boats from there, so that the army might be able to cross the river. But a sickness befalling him prevented the carrying out of the plan. 21.25. While Martinus and his men were using their shrinking from the crossing, and John's men were waiting for the instructions of Narses, in the meantime it befell that a great deal of time was spent in the siege. 21.26. And the besieged, now exceedingly hard pressed by famine and the evil overpowering them, most of them tasted of dogs and mice and of other animals which never came to the food of man. 21.27. So the barbarians, sending envoys to Mundilas, ordered him to give over the city to them, on condition that he himself and the soldiers should remain unharmed. 21.28. And he agreed to do this, if those men should both give pledges on their behalf and that they would do nothing unpleasant to any of the inhabitants. 21.29. But when the enemy gave pledges to Mundilas and the soldiers, while it was clear that, being gripped by much anger against the Ligurians, they would destroy them all, Mundilas, calling together all the soldiers, spoke as follows: 21.30. “If ever any others, when it was in their power to live shamefully, chose rather to die gloriously, exchanging an honourable end of life for immediate safety, such men at the present time I should wish you also to be, and not, through love of life, to pursue a life with shame, and this too, from the teaching of Belisarius, in which, having shared from of old, it is unholy for you not to be noble and exceedingly bold. 21.31. For to all who come into the light one fortune comes forth, to die at the appointed times; but in the manner of death men for the most part differ from one another. 21.32. And the difference is this, that cowards, as is natural, all owing insult and mockery to their enemies first, then none the less fulfil their fate at the times appointed from above, but to noble men it befalls to suffer this together with valour and an abundance of good repute. 21.33. And apart from these things, if it were in our power, while saving these people, to be slaves to the barbarians, this at least would bring some pardon for our shameful safety. 21.34. But if it is necessary to behold so great a multitude of Romans destroyed by the hands of the enemy, what would one call more bitter than this death? 21.35. For we should seem to be doing nothing else than helping the barbarians to accomplish the terrible deed. While, therefore, we are still masters of ourselves, let us adorn necessity with valour, and account the fortune that has fallen upon us a glorious one. 21.36. And I say that we ought, all of us being armed as best we can, to go against the enemy who are not expecting it. 21.37. For one of two things will be ours: either to have wrought through fortune something better than hope, or, having met with a happy end, to be most gloriously released from our present evils.” 21.38. Mundilas said so much, but none of the soldiers was willing to undertake the danger, but on the terms which the enemy proposed they gave over both themselves and the city. 21.39. And the barbarians, doing them no harm, kept them in custody together with Mundilas, but razed the city to the ground, killing all the males, no fewer than three hundred thousand, and making the women into the account of slaves, whom they gave to the Burgundians, repaying them thus for their alliance. 21.40. And finding Reparatus, the prefect of the court, they cut him into small pieces and threw his flesh to the dogs. 21.41. But Cervatinus (for he happened to be inside Mediolanum) was conveyed through Venetia and the nations there, together with his followers, to Dalmatia. And he came from there to the emperor, announcing this great disaster which had befallen the Romans. 21.42. And from this the Goths took the other cities by agreement which happened to have Roman garrisons, and again held the mastery over the whole of Liguria. And Martinus and Uliaris with the army returned to Rome.

22.1. These things, then, were thus. And Belisarius, who had not yet learned anything of what had happened in Liguria, when the winter was already ending, went with the whole army into Picenum. 22.2. And learning on this journey what had befallen Mediolanum, he made great mourning. 22.3. And he no longer permitted Uliaris to come into his sight for the future, but wrote to the emperor all that had happened. 22.4. But the emperor on account of these things did harm to no one, but, hearing of the disagreement between Belisarius and Narses, immediately summoned Narses and established Belisarius as supreme commander of the whole war. 22.5. Thus Narses returned to Byzantium, leading some few of the soldiers. But the Eruli no longer saw fit to remain in Italy when Narses withdrew from there, although Belisarius promised them that many good things would come to them from himself and from the emperor if they remained, but packing up they all first withdrew to Liguria. 22.6. There, falling in with the army of Uraïas, they sold to the enemy the slaves and other animals which they were bringing, and having received much money, they swore an oath never to array themselves against the Goths or to come to close quarters with them. 22.7. And thus making their withdrawal peaceful, they came to the regions about Venetia. There, joining Vitalius, they repented of their offences against the emperor Justinian. 22.8. And clearing themselves of the charge, they left Visandus, one of their commanders, with his followers there, while all the rest were conveyed to Byzantium, Aluith leading them and Philimuth, who, when Phanitheus had died at Caesena, held the command. 22.9. And Wittigis and the Goths with him, hearing that Belisarius would come against them and Ravenna at the beginning of spring, were in great fear and deliberated about their present situation; and after much deliberation (for they did not think themselves a match for the enemy by themselves) it seemed best to them to bring in the help of certain other barbarians. 22.10. From the Germans, then, having already had experience of their treachery and faithlessness, they abstained, being content if those men should not themselves come with Belisarius against them, 22.11. but should stand out of the way of both. And to the ruler of the Lombards, Vaces, they sent envoys, offering great sums of money and inviting them to alliance. 22.12. But these, when they learned that Vaces was a friend and ally to the emperor, withdrew without accomplishing anything. 22.13. So Wittigis, being at a loss before the present situation, as was natural, kept calling together many of the elders. From these he inquired frequently what course, in deliberating and acting, would make his affairs better. 22.14. So many opinions were spoken by those who came together for the deliberation, some in no way suited to the present situation, but others bringing something even worthy of account. 22.15. Among which this also came into the discussion, that never before had an emperor of the Romans been able to make war on the barbarians in the West, except indeed when a truce had been made with the Persians. 22.16. For both the Vandals and the Moors had then been destroyed, and the present disasters had befallen the Goths. So that, if anyone now also should set the king of the Medes against the emperor Justinian, the Romans, this nation being made hostile to them, would never thereafter be able to carry on another war against any men. 22.17. This pleased both Wittigis himself and the other Goths. It was resolved, therefore, to send envoys to Chosroes the king of the Medes—not Goths, however, in order that, becoming evident at once from this, they might not confound the matter, but Romans, who should make him hostile to the emperor Justinian. 22.18. Wherefore they persuaded with much money two of the priests in Liguria to this service. 22.19. Of whom the one, who seemed the more worthy, putting on the appearance and name of a bishop, though it in no way belonged to him, was appointed to the embassy, while the other followed him as his attendant. 22.20. And putting into their hands a letter written to Chosroes, Wittigis sent them. By these Chosroes, being moved, wrought irreparable deeds against the Romans during a truce, as I have related in the previous narrative. 22.21. But when the emperor Justinian heard that Chosroes and the Persians were deliberating these things, he resolved to bring the war in the West to an end as quickly as possible and to recall Belisarius, that he might march against the Persians. 22.22. So the envoys of Wittigis (for they happened to be still in Byzantium) he immediately sent away, promising that men would be sent by him to Ravenna who should make the truce with the Goths in whatever way might prove advantageous to both. 22.23. But Belisarius did not release these envoys to the enemy before they too released Athanasius and Peter and their men. 22.24. And when these had come to Byzantium, the emperor deemed them worthy of the greatest honours, establishing Athanasius as prefect of the praetorian guards in Italy, and granting to Peter the office of the so-called Master. 22.25. And the winter was ending, and the fourth year of this war which Procopius has written was coming to a close.

23.1. And Belisarius wished first to take Auximus and Fisula, and thus to go against Wittigis and Ravenna, no enemy being any longer able either to stand in his way or to do mischief behind him. 23.2. So Cyprianus and Justinus with their followers and some of the Isaurians he sent to Fisula, and five hundred foot-soldiers from the regiment which Demetrius commanded, who, encamping about the fort, besieged the barbarians there. 23.3. And Martinus and John with their followers and another army, which John commanded—whom they called also Phagas—he sent to the river Padus. 23.4. And he ordered them to take care that Uraïas and his men should not come against them from Mediolanum, but if they should not be able to repel the assault of the enemy, to follow them secretly behind and come upon their rear. 23.5. And they, occupying the city of Dorthona, which is by the river and without a wall, encamped and remained there, while he himself came to the city of Auximus, having eleven thousand men. 23.6. Now this Auximus is the first of the cities in Picenum, which the Romans have been accustomed to call its capital. And it is distant about eighty-four stades from the shore of the Ionian Gulf, and from the city of Ravenna a journey of three days and eighty stades. 23.7. And it lies on a certain high hill, having no entrance on the level ground, and from this it is altogether inaccessible to the enemy. 23.8. There Wittigis had established as garrison whatever was of repute among the Goths, judging that the Romans, if they did not first take this, would never dare to march against Ravenna. 23.9. And when the Roman army came to Auximus, Belisarius ordered all to encamp in a circle about the lower parts of the hill. 23.10. And they, gathering in companies, pitched their huts here and there about the place; but the Goths, observing them to be at a long distance from one another and not easily able to come to one another's aid, since it was a great plain, suddenly about late afternoon advanced against the enemy, toward the parts to the east of the city, where Belisarius happened to be still making a camp with his guards and shield-bearers. 23.11. And they, taking up their arms from what was at hand, defended themselves against the assailants, and very easily thrusting them back by their valour, routed them, and pursuing the fugitives came to the middle of the hill. 23.12. There the barbarians, turning about and trusting in the strength of the place, stood facing the pursuers, and shooting them from above killed many, until night, coming on, prevented them. So, separating, both sides bivouacked that night. 23.13. Now it happened that on the day before this action some of the Goths had been sent at deep dawn to the regions there for the gathering of provisions. 23.14. And these, having learned nothing about the presence of the enemy, returned at nightfall. And suddenly catching sight of the fires of the Romans, they came into great wonder and fear. 23.15. And many of them, daring to undertake the danger and escaping the notice of the enemy, entered Auximus. But all who, being terrified, immediately hid themselves in certain woods, in order to go to Ravenna, these, not long afterward coming under the power of their opponents, were destroyed. 23.16. And Belisarius, observing that Auximus was most strong in its safe position, and that it was altogether impossible for him to make an assault on the wall, thought he would never take the place by force, but he had hope, by a strict siege, of bringing the enemy into want of necessities and of making them subject in time. 23.17. Not far from the wall the earth, sending up much herbage, brought every day an occasion of engagement to the Romans and the Goths. 23.18. For when the Romans saw their opponents always cutting this for the sake of their horses, going up onto the hill at a run, and coming to close quarters with the enemy, and displaying deeds worthy of valour, they by no means allowed them to carry off the herbage, and always destroyed many of their opponents in this place. 23.19. And the barbarians, being worsted by the valour of the enemy, devised the following. Taking off the wheels of the wagons with the axles alone, they kept them in readiness, and beginning to cut the herbage, when they saw the Romans now coming up into the middle of the hill, they let the wheels go to rush down upon them from the height. 23.20. But by some chance it befell that these wheels came down to the level ground without touching any man. So having failed in this attempt, the barbarians for the moment fled inside the wall, but afterward did as follows. 23.21. Setting an ambush of their notable men in the ravines which are close to the wall, a few of them showed themselves to the enemy about the herbage; and when the battle was at close quarters, those who were hidden, leaping out of the ambushes, both far surpassing their opponents in numbers and dismaying them because they had not perceived it beforehand, killed very many and always turned the rest to flight. 23.22. And those of the Romans who stood in the camps saw the enemy rising from the ambushes, but, calling their comrades with much shouting, accomplished nothing, since the combatants by no means heard their cry, being separated from them by the length of the hill, and the barbarians always on purpose clashing their arms against them. 23.23. And while Belisarius was at a loss before the present situation, Procopius, who wrote this, coming to him, said: “Those who anciently used trumpets in the Roman army, O general, understood two notes, of which the one resembled most a command bidding the soldiers rush to battle, while the other called the combatants back to the camp, whenever this seemed best to the general. 23.24. And in this way the generals always ordered the soldiers what was fitting, and they were able to carry out the deeds enjoined. 23.25. For a shout in engagements is in no way able to signify anything clearly, since a din, as is natural, resounds everywhere, and fear confounds the senses of the combatants. 23.26. But since at the present time, through ignorance, such an art has slipped away, and it is impossible with a single trumpet to make both signals clear, do you henceforth do as follows. 23.27. With the cavalry trumpets command the soldiers to fight the enemy, and with the infantry trumpets call the men back to the retreat. 23.28. For it is impossible for them not to understand each of the two sounds, since the one comes from leather and exceedingly thin wood, the other from some thick bronze.” 23.29. Procopius said so much. And Belisarius was pleased with the suggestion, and calling the whole army together, spoke as follows: “Eagerness for this work I think both advantageous and worthy of much praise, so long as, being moderate, it brings no harm to those who have it. 23.30. For by excess all good things are wont always to turn to the worse. Do you, then, no longer be tripped up by contentiousness; for there is no shame in fleeing one who is doing mischief. 23.31. But he who goes unconsidered into manifest evil and is saved from it, if so it chance, incurs the charge of folly; but he is noble who plays the man in necessities. 23.32. The barbarians, then, since they are not able to fight us in the open, undertake to destroy us by ambushes. But for us to undertake the danger is more blameworthy than to escape their ambush. 23.33. For there is nothing more shameful than to yield to the designs of the enemy. For me, then, it will be a care that you do not fall into the ambushes of the enemy. 23.34. But it would be your task, whenever I give the signal, to go quickly to the retreat. And this signal for you will be from the infantry trumpet, O soldiers.” Belisarius said so much. 23.35. And the soldiers, observing the enemy about the herbage, went against them at a run, and killed some of them in the first charge. 23.36. Among whom one of the Moors, seeing one wearing gold, and laying hold of the hairs on his head in order to strip him, kept dragging the corpse. 23.37. But a certain Goth, hitting him with a javelin and chancing to strike both the muscles which are behind the shins, by the fixing of the javelin bound both his feet together. 23.38. But none the less the Moor, holding to the hairs, kept dragging the corpse. And in the meantime the barbarians set their ambushes in motion, and Belisarius, seeing from the camp what was being done, ordered the infantry whose task this was to sound their trumpets quickly. 23.39. And the Romans, perceiving this, now little by little began to withdraw, taking up the Moor with the javelin. And the Goths no longer dared to follow them, but withdrew without accomplishing anything.

24.1. As time went on and the want of provisions among the barbarians advanced greatly, they deliberated to report their situation to Wittigis. 24.2. And since none of them dared to set out on this task (for they thought they would never escape the notice of the besiegers), they devised the following. 24.3. Watching for a moonless night and making ready the men whom they purposed to send to Wittigis, and putting letters into their hands, when it was far into the night, they all shouted out prodigiously at many parts of the wall. 24.4. One would have guessed that they had fallen into confusion, the enemy pressing hard upon them and the city being taken contrary to expectation; 24.5. but the Romans, being altogether unable to conjecture what was happening, by the resolve of Belisarius remained quiet in the camps, suspecting both that there would be some plot from the city and that an army had come from Ravenna to the aid of the enemy and was coming against them. Fearing these things, they thought it better for them to be saved by remaining quiet in safety than to go into manifest danger on a moonless night. 24.6. So thus the barbarians, escaping the notice of the enemy, sent the men to Ravenna. And they, coming into the sight of no enemy man, reached Wittigis on the third day and showed the letters. 24.7. And the writing made plain the following: “When, O king, you established us in the garrison at Auximus, you said that you were depositing in our keeping the keys both of Ravenna itself and of your kingdom. 24.8. Wherefore you charged us to guard with all our might, in order that we, on our part, might not give over the power of the Goths to the enemy, and you affirmed to us when we begged that you would come to our aid of your own accord with the whole army. 24.9. We, then, until now, fighting against both famine and Belisarius, have become faithful guardians of your kingdom, but you have by no means resolved to help us in any way whatever. 24.10. Consider, therefore, lest the Romans, taking Auximus and taking up the keys, which you here neglect though they lie before you, shut you off from all your possessions for the future.” So much the letter made plain. 24.11. And when Wittigis saw it brought to him, for the moment he sent the men back, promising that he would come to the aid of Auximus with the whole army of the Goths; but after much consideration he remained quiet. 24.12. For he both suspected that John and his men would follow behind and place them between two enemies, and thinking that there was a great force of warlike men with Belisarius, he fell into helpless fear. 24.13. But most of all the famine disturbed him, since he had nowhere from which he might furnish provisions for the army. 24.14. For the Romans, holding mastery of the sea and possessing the fort at Ancon, depositing all the necessities there from both Sicily and Calabria, easily brought them from there in due season. 24.15. But to the Goths, if they should march into the land of Picenum, perceiving that there would be no means of provisions, he fell into helplessness. 24.16. So the men who had been sent from Auximus to Wittigis brought back his promise, escaping the notice of the enemy, to Auximus, and strengthened the barbarians there with empty hopes. 24.17. And Belisarius, hearing these things from the deserters, ordered the guard to be kept still more strictly, in order that nothing of this kind might happen again. These things, then, were thus. 24.18. And Cyprianus and Justinus, besieging Fisula, were by no means able either to assault the wall or to go anywhere near it; for this fort was hard to approach from all sides. And as the barbarians often sallied out against them, being more willing to settle matters with them by battle than to be hard pressed by the want of necessities, the engagements at first were evenly matched; but afterward the Romans, now having the advantage, shut the enemy up within the wall and kept them safely guarded, 24.19. so that no one could go anywhere from there. So the barbarians, being in want of the necessities and at a loss before the present situation, sent secretly to Wittigis, begging him to help them as quickly as possible, since they could no longer hold out for any longer time. 24.20. And Wittigis ordered Uraïas with the army in Liguria to go to Ticinum; for thus he himself affirmed that he would come to the aid of the besieged with the whole power of the Goths. 24.21. And he did accordingly, and moving all the army with him, went to Ticinum; and crossing the river Padus they came somewhere near the camp of the Romans. 24.22. There they too encamped and sat facing the enemy, distant from them about sixty stades. And neither side began hostilities. 24.23. For to the Romans it seemed sufficient if they should stand in the way of their opponents, so as to prevent them from going against the besiegers; and the barbarians shrank from fighting the enemy there, reckoning that, if they should fail in this engagement, they would destroy all the affairs of the Goths. 24.24. For they would no longer be able, by joining Wittigis, to help the besieged together with him. With such a purpose both sides remained quiet.

25.1. In the meantime the Franks, hearing that both Goths and Romans had been worn down by the war, and thinking that on this account they would most easily win for themselves the most of Italy, made it a grievous thing that, while others carried on a war for so long a time about the rule of a land so near them, they themselves, remaining quiet, should stand out of the way of both. 25.2. So, immediately forgetting their oaths and agreements which a little before they had made both with the Romans and with the Goths (for this nation is the most faithless of all men in matters of good faith), gathering at once to the number of a hundred thousand, with Theudibert leading them, they marched into Italy, having some few horsemen about the leader, 25.3. who alone bore spears, while the rest, all foot-soldiers, had neither bows nor spears, but each bore a sword and a shield and one axe. The iron of this was thick and exceedingly sharp on both sides, while the wooden handle was very short. 25.4. This axe they are accustomed always to throw at a single signal in the first charge, and to break the shields of the enemy and to kill the men. 25.5. Thus the Franks, crossing the Alps which separate the Gauls and the Italians, came into Liguria. 25.6. And the Goths, who had before been distressed at their faithlessness, because, though promising for alliance both much land and great sums of money, the Franks had often by no means been willing to fulfil the promise, when they heard that Theudibert was present with a large army, rejoiced, being lifted up in their hopes to the highest degree, and thought they would for the future prevail over the enemy without a battle. 25.7. And the Germans, so long as they were in Liguria, did nothing unpleasant to the Goths, in order that no hindrance to the crossing of the Padus might come to them from these men. 25.8. But when they came to the city of Ticinum, where the ancient Romans had built a bridge over this river, those who guarded it both served them in other ways and let them cross the Padus at their will. 25.9.
