And laying hold of the bridge, the Franks sacrificed the children and women of the Goths whom they found there and threw their bodies into the river as the first-fruits of the war. 25.10. For these barbarians, although they have become Christians, preserve the most of their ancient belief, using sacrifices of human beings and other unholy offerings, and by this they make their divinations. 25.11. And the Goths, observing what was being done, fell into helpless fear and, gripped by flight, got inside the wall. So the Germans, having crossed the river Padus, came to the camp of the Goths, and the Goths at first gladly watched them coming against them in small numbers, supposing that the men had come for their alliance. 25.12. But when a great throng of Germans poured in and set to work and, hurling their axes, were already doing much harm, the Goths, turning their backs, rushed into flight, and going through the camp of the Romans, ran toward Ravenna. 25.13. And the Romans, seeing them fleeing, supposed that Belisarius had come to their aid and had taken the camp of the enemy and was driving them out, having conquered in battle. Wishing to join him, they took up their arms and went quickly. 25.14. But falling unexpectedly upon an army of the enemy, they came to close quarters by no means willingly, and being defeated by far in the battle, they were no longer able to return to the camp, but all fled toward Tuscany. 25.15. And when they were now in safety, they reported all that had befallen them to Belisarius. 25.16. And the Franks, having conquered both, as has been said, and taken both camps altogether destitute of men, for the moment found provisions there, but in a short time having consumed all because of their multitude, they had nothing else to bring to themselves in a land destitute of men, except oxen and the water of the Padus. 25.17. And being unable to digest this meat with the abundance of water, most of them were seized by flux of the stomach and the disease of dysentery, from which they were by no means able to free themselves through the want of provisions. 25.18. They say, then, that the third part of the Frankish army perished in this way. Wherefore, being by no means able to go forward, they remained where they were. 25.19. And Belisarius, hearing both that the army of the Franks was present and that Martinus and John, defeated in battle, had fled, fell into helplessness, fearing both for the whole army and especially for those who were besieging at Fisula, since he learned that these barbarians were especially closer to them. He immediately wrote to Theudibert as follows: 25.20. “For a man who lays claim to virtue not to be false, especially the ruler of nations so many in number, I think, O noble Theudibert, 25.21. is not seemly. But to disregard, by wronging oaths written down, the agreements would not befit even the most dishonoured of men. These things you yourself at the present time know that you are doing wrong, although you agreed lately that you would help us in this war against the Goths. 25.22. But now you have not only stood out of the way of both, but have also so unconsideredly taken up arms and come against us. Do not you, most excellent man, thus insult a great emperor, who, I dare say, is not likely to requite the insult except in the greatest of measures. 25.23. And it is better for one to hold his own possessions in safety than, laying claim to what does not belong to him, to set himself into some danger concerning the most necessary things.” 25.24. When Theudibert had read this letter, being now both at a loss before the present situation and reproached by the Germans because they were dying from no cause in a deserted land, breaking up, he withdrew to his home with the survivors of the Franks with much speed.

26.1. Thus Theudibert, having marched into Italy, made his departure. And Martinus and John returned none the less, in order that the enemy might not make some assault upon those who were besieging. 26.2. But the Goths in Auximus, having learned nothing about the coming of the Franks, and despairing of the hope from Ravenna which was thus delaying, again purposed to call Wittigis to witness, but being unable to escape the guard of the enemy, they mourned. 26.3. After this, seeing one of the Romans, a Bessian by race, Burcentius by name, ranged under Narses the Armenian, alone keeping guard at midday, lest anyone from the city should go out to take the herbage, they came to a parley with him, coming nearer, and giving pledges that they would do him no harm, they bade him join them, promising that great sums of money would come to him from them. 26.4. And when they had come to the same place, the barbarians begged the man to convey a certain letter to Ravenna, fixing for him at once a stated sum of gold, and promising to give more when the letters of Wittigis should come back to them. 26.5. And the soldier, persuaded by the money, agreed to perform this and fulfilled the promise. So taking the sealed letters, he came quickly to Ravenna. And coming into the sight of Wittigis, he put the letter into his hands. 26.6. And it made plain the following: “In what condition our present affairs are you will know clearly by inquiring who in the world is the conveyer of the letter. 26.7. For it is impossible for a Goth to get outside the wall. And the most accessible of our foods is the herbage by the wall, of which we cannot now even touch as much as a little, unless we lose many in the struggle for it. To what end these things will come for us you and the Goths in Ravenna must consider.” 26.8. When Wittigis had read this, he answered as follows: “Let no one think, O dearest of all men, that we have given up, nor that we have come to such a degree of baseness as to throw away the affairs of the Goths through carelessness. 26.9. For lately the preparation for the sally had been made by me as fully as possible, and Uraïas, summoned from Mediolanum with the whole army, had come. 26.10. But the assault of the Franks, falling upon us unexpectedly, has checked all our preparations, for which I would not justly bear the blame. 26.11. For whatever is greater than human power both grants to those who have failed to be free from blame, fortune always drawing to herself the charges arising from what has been done. 26.12. Now, however (for we hear that Theudibert has been removed from our path), we shall be with you not long hence, God willing, with the whole army of the Goths. 26.13. And you ought to bear what befalls you both manfully and in a way suited to the necessity, reckoning your valour, for the sake of which I selected you from all and established you in Auximus, and respecting the reputation in which all the Goths, holding you in regard, have set you forth as a defence both of Ravenna 26.14. and of their own safety.” Having written so much, Wittigis presented the man with much money and sent him away. And he, coming to Auximus, went to his comrades, and pretending that some sickness had befallen him, and that on this account he had been idling at a certain church not far off, he again took his station at the watch where he was wont, and, escaping the notice of all, gave the letters to the enemy; which, being read aloud to the multitude, strengthened all still more, 26.15. although they were hard pressed by famine. Wherefore they were by no means willing to come over to Belisarius, who was constantly trying to win them. And again (for no army was reported to have come out from Ravenna for them, and they were now prodigiously distressed by the want of necessities) they sent Burcentius once more, making plain only this in the letter, that within five days they were no longer able to fight against the famine. And he returned to them again, having a letter of Wittigis that buoyed them up with the same hopes. 26.16. But the Romans, none the less distressed because they had made the siege so long in a deserted land, were at a loss, seeing the barbarians not giving in to them amid so many evils. 26.17. Wherefore Belisarius was eager to take alive one of the notable men among the enemy, in order that he might learn for what reason the barbarians were enduring these terrors, and Valerianus agreed to perform such a thing for him easily. 26.18. For he said there were some among his followers of the nation of the Sclaveni, who are accustomed to hide themselves behind a small stone or any chance bush and snatch up an enemy man. 26.19. And this they always display by the river Ister, where they are settled, both against the Romans and against the other barbarians. Belisarius was pleased with the proposal and ordered him to attend to the matter quickly. 26.20. So Valerianus, selecting one of the Sclaveni who was well off in greatness of body and exceedingly energetic, instructed him to bring an enemy man, affirming that great rewards would be his from Belisarius. 26.21. And he said he would do this easily in the place where the herbage happens to be; for the Goths for a long time, in want of necessities, were feeding there. 26.22. So the Sclavenian, coming at deep dawn close to the wall, hiding himself in a certain bush and drawing his body into a small space, lay concealed about the herbage. 26.23. And at daybreak a Goth came there and quickly began gathering the plants, suspecting nothing unpleasant from the bush, but looking frequently toward the camp of the enemy, lest anyone should come from there against him. 26.24. And the Sclavenian, falling upon him suddenly from behind, snatched him up, gripping the man firmly with both hands around the middle, and carried him into the camp, and bringing him put him into the hands of Valerianus. 26.25. And when he inquired in whom the Goths were trusting and what stronghold they had that they were by no means willing to come over to them, but willingly held out against the most terrible things, the barbarian told the whole story about Burcentius and convicted him to his face when he came into his sight. 26.26. And Burcentius, when he perceived that he had already become known, hid nothing of what had been done. Wherefore Belisarius gave him over to his comrades to deal with as they wished, and they not long afterward burnt him alive, the enemy watching what was being done. Thus Burcentius reaped the fruit of his love of money.

27.1. And Belisarius, seeing that the barbarians were holding out against the hardship none the less, purposed to set the plot against the water, thinking that in this way he would take the enemy more easily and with less trouble. 27.2. And, since there was a certain spring of Auximus toward the north wind in a precipitous place, distant about a stone's throw from the wall, which let its stream little by little into a certain cistern there from of old, and the cistern, having become full from this small inflow, allowed those in Auximus to draw water with no toil—a thought came to Belisarius that, if the water did not collect there, the barbarians, being shot at by the enemy, would never be able in a long time to fill their jars from the inflow. 27.3. Wishing, then, to destroy the cistern, he devised the following. Arming the whole army, and drawing it up in a circle about the wall as if for battle, he gave his opponents the impression that he was about immediately to assault the wall from all sides. 27.4. Wherefore the Goths, dreading the assault, remained quiet on the battlements, intending to defend themselves from there against the enemy. 27.5. In the meantime Belisarius brought into the cistern five Isaurians experienced in building, with axes and other tools suited for the cutting of stones, hidden by a multitude of shields, and ordered them to destroy and break up the walls with all their might quickly. 27.6. And the barbarians for a while suspected that the men were going against the wall, and kept quiet, in order that, when they should come very close, they might shoot them easily, having no thought of what was being done; but when they saw the Isaurians inside the cistern, they hurled all their stones and arrows at them. 27.7. Then all the rest of the Romans withdrew at a run, but the five Isaurians alone, when they had got into safety, set to work; for a vault had been made over the water for the sake of shade by the men of old there. 27.8. And getting inside this, they took no heed of the enemy, although they shot many missiles. 27.9. Wherefore the Goths no longer endured to remain inside the wall, but opening the postern there, all went against the Isaurians, gripped by much anger and tumult. 27.10. And the Romans, Belisarius urging them on, met them with much eagerness. So a fierce battle took place, having for a long time a shoving and much slaughter on both sides. 27.11. But of the Romans more in number fell. For the barbarians, defending themselves from above, few though they were, overpowered many, and prevailing in the shoving, killed more than they themselves died. 27.12. The Romans, however, were by no means willing to give in, ashamed before Belisarius who was present and urging them on with shouting. 27.13. Then indeed a missile came at the belly of the general with a great rush, from one of the enemy, whether by some chance or by design shot at that point. 27.14. This Belisarius did not at all see. For he was able neither to guard against it nor to turn aside in any way. But a certain guard, Unigastus by name, standing by him, perceived it not far from the belly of Belisarius, and throwing forward his right hand, saved the general from the unexpected, but himself, struck by the arrow, immediately, being in great pain, withdrew. 27.15. And afterward, the tendons being cut, he was no longer able to use the hand. And the battle, having begun in the morning, came to midday. 27.16. And seven Armenian men, ranged under Narses and Aratius, displayed deeds worthy of valour, running about the difficult ground, which was most steep, as if on the level, and killing those of the enemy who always withstood them, until, thrusting back the barbarians there, they routed them. 27.17. And the rest of the Romans, seeing the enemy now giving in, pursued them, and the rout became brilliant, and the barbarians got inside the wall again. 27.18. So the Romans thought that the cistern had been destroyed and that the whole work had been accomplished by the Isaurians, but they had not been able to take away even so much as a pebble from there. 27.19. For the ancient craftsmen, taking the greatest care for valour in their works, had so wrought this structure too that it yielded neither to time nor to the plotting of men. 27.20. So the Isaurians, having accomplished nothing, when they saw the Romans masters of the place, departing from the cistern, withdrew to the camp. 27.21. Wherefore Belisarius ordered the soldiers to throw into the water the dead bodies of animals and herbs of a kind naturally sufficient for the destruction of man, and to throw in there and slake quicklime burnt most thoroughly (which they anciently were accustomed to call titanos, but now asbestos). 27.22. And they did so, but the barbarians during this time used a well inside the wall which had a very small amount of water, in less measure than their need. 27.23. And for the rest Belisarius was eager neither to take the place by force nor to display any plot concerning water or anything else, having the hope of prevailing over the enemy by famine alone. 27.24. And from this he most strongly attended to the guard. And the Goths, still waiting for the army from Ravenna, kept quiet in much want of the necessities. 27.25. And now the besieged in Fisula were most hard pressed by famine, and being unable to bear the evil, and despairing also of the hope from Ravenna, resolved to come over to their opponents. 27.26. So coming to a parley with Cyprianus and Justinus, and taking pledges concerning their lives, they surrendered both themselves and the fort by agreement. And Cyprianus and his men, taking them along with the Roman army, and establishing a sufficient garrison in Fisula, came to Auximus. 27.27. And Belisarius, constantly showing their commanders to the barbarians in Auximus, exhorted them to let go of their madness, shaking off the hope from Ravenna; for there would never be any profit for them either, but, after being most grievously worn down by hardship, they would none the less come to the same fortune as those in Fisula. 27.28. And they, after much deliberation among themselves, since they could no longer hold out against the famine, admitted his words and saw fit to surrender the city, on condition that they themselves should march to Ravenna unharmed with their goods. 27.29. Wherefore Belisarius was at a loss before the present situation, thinking it inexpedient that enemies of such valour and such numbers should mingle with those in Ravenna, but being by no means willing to be too late for the opportunity, and to go against Ravenna and Wittigis while affairs were still in suspense. 27.30. For the Franks disturbed him, being very likely to come immediately to the help of the Goths. Being eager to forestall their coming, he was unable to break off the siege while Auximus was not yet taken. 27.31. And the soldiers would not allow him to concede their goods to the barbarians, displaying the many wounds which they had received there from them, and enumerating all the toils that had befallen them in this siege, of which, they affirmed, the spoils of the conquered were the prizes. 27.32. At last both the Romans, compelled by the sharpness of the opportunity, and the Goths, forced by famine, came to an agreement with one another, on condition that the Romans should distribute half of the goods among themselves, and the Goths, keeping the remainder, should be subjects of the emperor. 27.33. Both, then, gave pledges concerning these things—the commanders of the Romans that the agreements should be binding, and the Goths that they would hide nothing whatever of the goods. 27.34. And thus they distributed all the goods, and the Romans held Auximus, and the barbarians mingled with the emperor's army.

28.1. And when Belisarius had taken Auximus, he was eager to besiege Ravenna and led the whole army there. And sending Magnus with a large multitude beyond Ravenna, he ordered him always to go about the bank of the river Padus and keep guard, in order that for the future the Goths might not bring in provisions from there. 28.2. And Vitalius too, coming to him with an army from Dalmatia, guarded the other bank of the river. There befell them a certain chance, making manifest at once that fortune herself directs the affairs of both sides. 28.3. For the Goths, having before collected many boats in Liguria, had let them down into the Padus, intending, after filling them with grain and the other provisions, to sail to Ravenna. 28.4. But the water of this river at that time so failed that it was altogether impossible to sail upon it, until the Romans, coming up, took the boats with all their cargoes. 28.5. And the river not long afterward, returning to its proper flow, became navigable again for the rest of the time. And we know by report that this never happened to it before. 28.6. And now the barbarians began to be in want of provisions. For they could neither bring anything in through the Ionian Gulf, the enemy holding mastery of the sea everywhere, and they had been shut off from the river. 28.7. And the rulers of the Franks, perceiving what was being done, and wishing to make Italy their own, sent envoys to Wittigis, offering a promise of alliance, 28.8. on condition that they should rule the land together with him. When Belisarius heard this, he too sent envoys to oppose the Germans, among others Theodosius, who was set over his own household. 28.9. So first the envoys of the Germans, coming into the sight of Wittigis, spoke as follows: “The rulers of the Germans have sent us, being distressed because they have heard that you are being besieged by Belisarius, and being eager to help you as quickly as possible according to the alliance. 28.10. Now we think that an army of fighting men no fewer than fifty thousand has already crossed the Alps, with whom we boast that we shall overwhelm the whole Roman army with our axes in the first charge. 28.11. And you it behoves to follow in purpose not those who would enslave you, but those who set themselves to the danger of war out of goodwill toward the Goths. 28.12. And besides, if you take up arms with us, no hope will be left to the Romans of coming to close quarters with both armies, but from the very outset, with no toil, we shall bind on the mastery of the war. 28.13. But if the Goths array themselves with the Romans, not even so will they hold out against the nation of the Franks (for the contest will not be of equal forces), but it will be your lot to be defeated along with the bitterest enemies of all. 28.14. And to go to manifest evil, when it is possible to be saved free from danger, is much folly. And altogether the race of the Romans is faithless to all barbarians, since it is by nature hostile. 28.15. We, then, will rule the whole of Italy together with you, if you wish, and will administer the land in whatever way may seem best. But it is fitting for you and the Goths to choose whatever is going to be advantageous to you.” The Franks said so much. 28.16. And the envoys of Belisarius, coming forward, spoke as follows: “That the multitude of Germans, with which these men see fit to frighten you, will do no harm to the emperor's army, why should one speak at length among you, to whom, through long experience, it has befallen to know thoroughly every turn of war, and that valour is least wont to be inferior to a throng of men? 28.17. For we forbear to say that to the emperor above all it is possible to prevail over the enemy by a multitude of soldiers. And the good faith of these men, which they boast they use toward all barbarians, except indeed the Thuringians and the nation of the Burgundians, has been displayed by them toward you their allies. 28.18. For we would gladly ask the Franks by what god they intend to swear that they affirm they will give the assurance of good faith to you. 28.19. For the god already sworn by them, in what manner they have honoured him, you doubtless know; they who, having received such great sums of money, and all the Gauls, from you for alliance, not only by no means resolved to share the danger with you, but also took up arms so wantonly against you, if any account survives among you of what happened by the Padus. 28.20. And what need is there, by mentioning what is past, to convict the impiety of the Franks? Nothing could be more abominable than their present embassy. 28.21. For, as if having forgotten what they themselves agreed and swore by the treaties, they see fit to share everything in common with you. 28.22. And if they should obtain this too from you, to what end the insatiableness of their love of money will come for them, it is fitting to consider.” 28.23. So much the envoys of Belisarius also said. And Wittigis, after much consultation with the best of the Goths, chose the agreements with the emperor and dismissed the envoys of the Germans without accomplishing anything. And for the rest the Goths and Romans now treated with one another, but Belisarius none the less kept watch that the barbarians might not bring in provisions. 28.24. And he ordered Vitalius, going into Venetia, to bring in as much as possible of the places there, while he himself, sending Ildiger, guarded the Padus on both sides, in order that the barbarians might the more, through want of necessities, give in and make the agreements in the way he wished. 28.25. And when he learned that much grain was still stored in public buildings inside Ravenna, he persuaded with money one of the inhabitants there to set fire secretly to these buildings together with the grain. 28.26. And they say that these things were destroyed by the resolve of Matasuntha, the wife of Wittigis. And when the grain had been suddenly burnt, some suspected that the deed had been done by design, while others suspected that the place had been struck by lightning. 28.27. And reckoning both, the Goths and Wittigis fell into helplessness still more, no longer able to trust even themselves and thinking that they were being warred upon by God. These things, then, were thus done. 28.28. In the Alps which separate the Gauls and the Ligurians, which the Romans call the Cottian Alps, there happen to be many forts. 28.29. There Goths, many and excellent, settled from of old together with their wives and children, held the guard, whom, when Belisarius heard that they wished to come over to him, he sent one of his followers, Thomas by name, with some few men, in order that, giving pledges, they might win over the barbarians there by agreement. 28.30. And when they had come to the Alps, Sisigis, who commanded the watch-stations there, receiving them in one of the forts, both came over himself and induced each of the others to this. 28.31. In the meantime Uraïas, selecting four thousand from the Ligurians and from the forts in the Alps, went quickly to Ravenna to help. 28.32. And these, when they learned what Sisigis had done, fearing for their own families, 28.33. saw fit to go there first. Wherefore Uraïas went with the whole army to the Cottian Alps and besieged Sisigis together with Thomas and his men. And when John, the nephew of Vitalian, and Martinus learned this (for they happened to be very close to the river Padus), they quickly came to the aid with the whole army, and falling by a sudden raid upon some of the forts in the Alps, took them, and enslaved those who dwelt there, among whom it befell that there were many children and wives of those serving under Uraïas. 28.34. For very many of them, setting out from these forts, followed him. 28.35. And these, when they learned that their own families had been taken, deserting the camp of the Goths suddenly, resolved to come over to John and his men, and from this Uraïas was able neither to accomplish anything there nor to help the Goths in danger in Ravenna, but coming with a few men to Liguria without accomplishing anything, remained quiet. And Belisarius at his ease shut up Wittigis and the notable Goths in Ravenna.

29.1. And then envoys came from the emperor, Domnicus and Maximinus, both of senatorial rank, in order to make peace on the following terms: 29.2. that Wittigis should carry off half of the royal wealth, and should rule the land which is beyond the river Padus; and that half of the goods should be the emperor's, and that he should make subject in the payment of tribute all that is within the river Padus. 29.3. And the envoys, showing the emperor's letters to Belisarius, were conveyed to Ravenna. And when the Goths and Wittigis had learned for what they had come, they gladly agreed to make the treaty on these terms. 29.4. When Belisarius heard this, he was distressed, regarding it as a great misfortune if anyone should not allow him, when it was possible with no toil, both to win the mastery of the whole war and to lead Wittigis a captive to Byzantium. 29.5. And when the envoys came to him from Ravenna, he was by no means willing to confirm the agreements with letters of his own. 29.6. The Goths, perceiving this, suspected that the Romans were offering them peace with treacherous intent, and used great suspicion toward them, and now declared openly that without the letters and oaths of Belisarius they would never make a treaty with them. 29.7. And Belisarius, hearing that some of the commanders reviled him as plotting against the emperor's affairs and being by no means willing to bring the war to an end, called all together, in the presence of Domnicus and Maximinus, and spoke as follows: 29.8. “That the fortune of war stands least of all in safety, I myself know, and I think that each of you knows the same as I about it. 29.9. For the hope of victory, when it is most expected to come to them, has tripped up many, and to those who seemed to have been unfortunate among their enemies it has befallen, contrary to expectation, to survive. 29.10. Wherefore I say that those who deliberate about peace ought not to put forward the good hope alone, but to keep in mind that the issue will be on either side, and thus to make the choice of their resolve. 29.11. These things being so, it seemed best to me to bring in you my fellow-commanders and these envoys of the emperor, in order that, choosing freely at the present time whatever may seem advantageous to the emperor, you may never afterward make any reproach against me concerning these affairs. 29.12. For it would be most absurd to keep silent while it is possible to choose the better course, but, when looking to the issue of fortune, to make accusations. 29.13. What, then, has been resolved by the emperor and is desired by Wittigis for the ending of the war, you doubtless know. 29.14. But if these things seem advantageous to you too, let each one come forward and say so. If, however, you think you are able to recover the whole of Italy for the Romans and to gain the mastery over the enemy, nothing will hinder you from saying it, holding back nothing.” When Belisarius had said this, 29.15. all openly declared that the emperor's plans were best, and that they would not be able to do the enemy any further harm. 29.16. And Belisarius, pleased with the opinion of the commanders, saw fit that they should make it plain in writing, in order that they might never deny it. And they, writing it in a little book, made plain that they were not able to prevail in the war over their opponents. 29.17. These things were happening in the Roman camp. But the Goths, hard pressed by famine and no longer able to hold out against the hardship, were distressed with the rule of Wittigis, as having been most unfortunate, but shrank from coming over to the emperor, fearing nothing else than lest, having become slaves of the emperor, they should be compelled to remove from Italy and, going to Byzantium, to settle there. 29.18. Deliberating, then, among themselves, whatever was uncorrupt among the Goths, they resolved to proclaim Belisarius emperor of the West. And sending to him secretly, they begged him to set himself in the kingship; for in this way they affirmed they would gladly follow him. 29.19. But Belisarius was by no means willing to set himself in power without the will of the emperor; 29.20. for he was prodigiously distressed at the name of tyrant, and had previously been bound by the most dreadful oaths to the emperor that he would never, while he lived, attempt a revolution. But in order that he might manage the present situation as well as possible, he resolved gladly to admit the words of the barbarians. 29.21. Perceiving this, Wittigis was afraid, and saying that the Goths had deliberated most excellently, he himself too secretly advised Belisarius to go into the kingship; 29.22. for no one would stand in his way. And then Belisarius again, calling together both the envoys of the emperor and all the commanders, asked whether it seemed to them worthy of much account to make all the Goths together with Wittigis captives, and to plunder all the goods, 29.23. and to recover the whole of Italy for the Romans. And they said this would be a lofty and prodigious piece of good fortune for the Romans, and saw fit for him to do whatever he was able as quickly as possible. 29.24. So immediately Belisarius sent some of his friends to Wittigis and the notable Goths, ordering them to fulfil what they had promised. 29.25. For the famine did not allow them to put off the matter to any other time, but, pressing still harder, urged them to this. 29.26. Wherefore they sent envoys to the Roman camp again, to say one thing to the multitude, but secretly to receive pledges from Belisarius that he would do harm to none of them, and that he himself for the future would be emperor over both the Italians and the Goths, and that thus he would come with them and the Roman army to Ravenna. 29.27. And Belisarius swore to all the other things, just as the envoys saw fit, but said that he would swear concerning the kingship to Wittigis himself and to the commanders of the Goths. 29.28. And the envoys, thinking that he would never reject the kingship but desired it above all things, ordered him immediately to go to Ravenna with them. 29.29. And then Belisarius ordered Bessas and John and Narses and Aratius (for these he suspected to be most ill-disposed to him) to go off, each in a different direction, with their followers, to provide themselves with the necessities; for he said it was no longer possible for him to bring provisions into this place for the whole army. 29.30. And they did so, together with Athanasius the prefect of the praetorian guards, who had just come from Byzantium; while he himself with the rest of the army went with the envoys of the Goths to Ravenna. 29.31. And filling a fleet of ships with grain and the other provisions, he ordered them to sail quickly into the harbour of Classes; for so the Romans call the suburb of Ravenna where the harbour is. 29.32. And to me at that time, as I observed the entrance of the Roman army into Ravenna, a thought came that affairs are accomplished by no means through the wisdom of men or any other excellence, but that there is a certain divine power which always turns their minds and leads them there, where there will be no hindrance to the things being accomplished. 29.33. For the Goths, far surpassing their opponents in numbers and power, and neither settled by battle, since they were in Ravenna, nor enslaved in spirit by anything else whatever, became captives of those inferior to them and held the name of slavery in no insult at all. 29.34. And the women (for they happened to have heard from their husbands that the enemy were great in body and superior in number), when they saw all of them sitting at the gate, spat in the faces of their husbands, all of them, and pointing with their hands at the victors, reproached them for their cowardice. 29.35. And Belisarius kept Wittigis in custody, not without honour, but ordered those of the barbarians who dwelt within the river Padus, who were going to their own fields, 29.36. to attend to them at their will. For he suspected that no enemy would arise there, nor would the Goths ever combine there, since he had previously established many of the Roman army in those regions. And they went off quickly and gladly. 29.37. And thus the Romans were now in safety; for they were no longer worsted by the Goths in Ravenna in numbers. And after this he took the goods in the Palatium, which he was to convey to the emperor. 29.38. For he himself plundered none of the Goths, nor permitted anyone else to plunder, but each of them preserved his property according to the agreements. 29.39. And when those of the barbarians who held the guard in the strongest of the places heard that Ravenna and Wittigis were held by the Romans, they sent envoys to Belisarius, seeing fit to surrender both themselves by agreement and what they guarded. 29.40. And he, providing pledges to all most readily, won over Tarbesion and any other fortification there was in Venetia. For Caesena alone in Aemilia was left, which he had previously won over together with Ravenna. 29.41. And all the Goths who commanded these places, as soon as they received pledges, came to Belisarius and remained there; but Ildibadus, a man of repute, who commanded the garrison in Verona, sent envoys indeed to Belisarius on the same terms as the others, since Belisarius had found and held his children in Ravenna, yet he neither came to Ravenna nor became subject to Belisarius. For a certain fortune befell him which I shall presently make plain.

30.1. Some of the commanders of the Roman army, having envy toward Belisarius, slandered him to the emperor, bringing against him a charge of tyranny that in no way belonged to him. 30.2. But the emperor, not so much persuaded by these slanders, but because the Median war was now pressing upon him, summoned Belisarius as quickly as possible, in order that he might march against the Persians; and he ordered Bessas and John with the others to take care of Italy, and instructed Constantianus to go from Dalmatia to Ravenna. 30.3. And the Goths who were settled beyond the river Padus and Ravenna, hearing that the emperor was summoning Belisarius, at first regarded the matter as unreasonable, supposing that Belisarius would never set the kingship of Italy below his loyalty to Justinian. 30.4. But when they learned that the preparation for his departure was great, taking counsel together, whatever was still uncorrupt among them, they went to Ticinum to Uraïas the nephew of Wittigis, and after first weeping much with him, spoke as follows: 30.5. “No other has been more responsible for the present evils to the nation of the Goths than you. For we should long ago have removed your uncle, who led us so basely and unfortunately, from his rule, as we did Theudatus the nephew of Theoderic, had we not, out of respect for your seeming energy, resolved to concede to Wittigis the name of the kingship, but in deed to hand over to you alone the rule of the Goths. 30.6. But the goodwill that then seemed ours has turned about, now appearing as folly and the cause of these our misfortunes. 30.7. For of the Goths, as you know, O dear Uraïas, it befalls that most and the best have died in the war, and of the survivors, whatever best is left, Belisarius will go off taking, together with Wittigis and all the goods. 30.8. And that this same thing will befall us too a little later, being few and exceedingly pitiable, no one would gainsay. 30.9. With such terrors, then, standing about us, it will be more profitable to die with good repute than to behold our children and wives being led off by the enemy to the ends of the earth. 30.10. And we shall do something, as is likely, worthy of valour, if we have you as leader of our deeds.” The Goths said so much. 30.11. And Uraïas answered as follows: “That in the present terrors we ought to choose danger before slavery, it befalls me to think the same as you. 30.12. But for me to set myself in the kingship of the Goths I think altogether inexpedient; first, because, being the nephew of Wittigis, a man so unfortunate, I should seem contemptible to the enemy, since men think that like fortunes are always passed on to kinsmen; 30.13. and second, I should seem to be doing what is unholy, mounting to the rule of my uncle, and on this account I should, as is likely, have most of you distressed at me. 30.14. But I say that we ought to set Ildibadus into this danger as ruler of the Goths, a man who has come to the height of valour and is exceedingly energetic. 30.15. And it is not unlikely that Theudis, who is his uncle and the ruler of the Visigoths, will join in the war because of the kinship. Wherefore we shall carry on the contest against our opponents with better hope.” 30.16. Having said so much, Uraïas too seemed to all the Goths to be speaking what was advantageous. And Ildibadus came to them immediately, summoned from Verona. 30.17. And throwing the purple about him, they proclaimed him king of the Goths and begged him to set their present affairs well in order. Thus Ildibadus came into power. 30.18. And a little later, calling together all the Goths, he spoke as follows: “I know that all of you, fellow-soldiers, are experienced in many wars, so that we shall never with reason go straight to making war. For experience, bringing reckoning, is least wont to be bold. 30.19. And it is worth while for you, remembering all that has happened before, thus now to deliberate about the present. 30.20. For forgetfulness, coming upon many men of what has already gone before, has lifted up their thoughts not as it ought, through ignorance, 30.21. and has sufficiently tripped them up in the greatest matters. Wittigis, then, not against your will nor while you resisted, gave himself into the hands of the enemy, but having then given up before the oppositions of fortune, you thought it most advantageous for yourselves to sit at home and obey Belisarius, rather than to risk your bodies endlessly. 30.22. But now, having heard that he is being sent to Byzantium, you have resolved to undertake a revolution. And yet each of you ought to reckon that not all things turn out for men as they think, but the issue of affairs has often gone contrary to expectation, in the opposite direction to what was resolved. 30.23. For fortune and repentance are wont for the most part to set things right from the unexpected; and that this will happen now too to Belisarius is in no way unlikely. 30.24. It is better, then, first to inquire of him, and to try to set the man back to the agreements made before, and thus for you to proceed to the second course in your actions.” 30.25. When Ildibadus had said this, he seemed to the Goths to have deliberated well, and he sent envoys to Ravenna quickly. And these, coming into the sight of Belisarius, reminded him of the agreements made with them and reviled him as a breaker of what had been agreed, calling him a self-chosen slave, and reproaching him because he did not blush at choosing slavery before kingship, and saying many other such things, exhorted him to the rule. 30.26. For thus, they affirmed, Ildibadus too would come of his own accord, to lay down the purple at his feet and do obeisance to Belisarius as emperor of both Goths and Italians. 30.27. The envoys said these things, thinking that the man would draw to himself the name of kingship without any delay at once. 30.28. But he, contrary to their expectation, openly refused, saying that Belisarius would never, while the emperor Justinian lived, mount to the name of kingship. 30.29. And they, hearing this, departed as quickly as possible and reported the whole matter to Ildibadus. 30.30. And Belisarius went off toward Byzantium; and the winter was ending, and the fifth year of this war which Procopius has written was coming to a close.
